opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that it's really a train-test mismatch. In standard supervised distillation, you take a fixed dataset of sequences, either ground-truth outputs or samples generated by the teacher, and you train the student to imitate the teacher token by token on those sequences. The key thing is that during training, the student is always conditioned on prefixes it didn't produce. It's being teacher-forced on "good" contexts.

At inference time, though, the student generates autoregressively, so it conditions on its own previous tokens. The student is smaller and less capable, so it will inevitably make mistakes, and once it drifts slightly off the distribution of prefixes it saw during training, it's in territory where it never got any supervision. Errors compound. A small early mistake puts you in an unfamiliar state, which makes the next mistake more likely, and so on. That's exposure bias: the student was only ever exposed to the teacher's or the data's distribution over prefixes, never its own.

This is the same problem imitation learning has had for a long time. Behavioral cloning has exactly this compounding-error issue, and the classic fix there is something like DAgger, where you let the learner act, visit its own states, and then ask the expert what it would have done in those states.

That's essentially the intuition behind on-policy distillation, which we explored in our GKD work. Instead of training only on a fixed set of teacher outputs, you sample sequences from the student, then ask the teacher for its token-level distribution on those student-generated prefixes, and minimize some divergence between the two. The student gets feedback precisely on the mistakes it actually makes, so you close the gap between what it sees in training and what it sees at test time.

There's also a second, related issue: the choice of divergence. Standard supervised KD minimizes forward KL, which is mode-covering. A small student that can't represent everything the teacher does ends up spreading probability mass over regions the teacher wouldn't assign much probability to, and when you sample from it you get low-quality outputs. Things like reverse KL or generalized Jensen-Shannon divergences are more mode-seeking, letting the student focus on what it can do well. In practice, combining on-policy data with the right divergence gave us pretty substantial gains on things like summarization, translation, and math reasoning.

The other nice thing is that on-policy distillation fits naturally with RL fine-tuning. You're already sampling from the student, so you can add a reward term alongside the distillation loss. That's one way to see distillation and RLHF-style training as part of the same family of methods.

r001.rationale: It contrasts training on fixed teacher or ground-truth sequences with autoregressive generation from the student’s own tokens at inference.

r002.rationale: It explains that a student’s early mistakes can move it off the training-prefix distribution, where it has no supervision, causing further errors.

r003.rationale: It describes training on “good” teacher or data contexts and says the student gets no supervision on unfamiliar prefixes after its own mistakes, leaving it without guidance there.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that supervised distillation, at least the standard recipe, is really just supervised fine-tuning on teacher outputs. You take a big teacher model, you sample a bunch of completions from it, and then you train the student with next-token prediction on those completions. And the issue is exactly the same one that shows up in regular supervised learning for sequence models, which is that during training the student is always conditioned on the teacher's prefix. Every token it predicts, the context it sees is this perfect, teacher-generated context.

But at inference time the student is conditioned on its own prefix. It generates a token, then conditions on that, generates the next one, and so on. So if it makes a small mistake early, it's now in a state it never saw during training, because the teacher would never have produced that prefix. And the errors compound. That's the train-test mismatch people call exposure bias.

What I found interesting when we were working on this is that it's really a distribution-shift problem, and once you frame it that way the fix is kind of obvious: you want the student to be trained on its own samples. So instead of only using teacher-generated sequences, you sample from the student, and then you get feedback from the teacher on those samples, token by token, by matching the student's distribution to the teacher's distribution on student-generated prefixes. That's the on-policy piece. The student is seeing the states it will actually visit at inference time, and the teacher is telling it what to do in those states.

And the nice thing is the teacher doesn't have to actually generate anything. You just need its logits on the student's sequence, which is a forward pass, so it's quite cheap. You can also mix things up, use some teacher samples, some student samples, and you can play with the divergence, like forward KL versus reverse KL or some generalized version, because once you're matching distributions on your own samples, which divergence you pick actually starts to matter in terms of whether the student is mode-covering or mode-seeking.

So in short: exposure bias in distillation is the student learning from a distribution of states it will never be in, and on-policy distillation is basically the cure for that.

r001.rationale: It contrasts training on teacher-generated prefixes with inference on the student’s own autoregressive prefixes.

r002.rationale: It says an early student mistake creates a prefix absent from training because the teacher would not have produced it.

r003.rationale: It explains that teacher-generated contexts are successful contexts, so the student has not been trained on how to proceed after its own mistake; it then describes teacher feedback on student-generated states.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that, in supervised distillation, you train the student on trajectories generated by the teacher. At each step, the student sees a prefix from the teacher and learns to predict the next token. But at inference time, it’s conditioning on its own outputs.

If the student makes a slightly different choice, it can end up in a context that it never saw during training. And then mistakes can compound, because it hasn’t learned how to recover from its own errors. That mismatch between the training distribution and the distribution induced by the student is the exposure-bias problem.

So one way to address it is to let the student generate during training and get feedback from the teacher on those student-generated contexts. You’re teaching the student what to do in situations it actually encounters.

r001.rationale: It says training uses teacher-generated prefixes, while inference conditions on the student’s own outputs, creating a mismatch in distributions.

r002.rationale: It explains that a different student choice can lead to a context absent from training and that mistakes can compound.

r003.rationale: It says the student has not learned how to recover from its own errors because training used teacher-generated trajectories.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about exposure bias is that, during supervised distillation, the student learns to predict the teacher’s next token conditioned on a prefix the teacher produced. But at inference time, it’s conditioning on its own generations. Those are different distributions.

If the student makes a small mistake, it can end up with a prefix that it never encountered during training. And then it hasn’t necessarily learned how to recover, so errors can compound over a long generation.

That motivates on-policy distillation: let the student generate the prefixes, and have the teacher provide supervision on those prefixes. You’re teaching the student what to do in the states it actually visits, rather than only along the teacher’s trajectories.

r001.rationale: It contrasts training on teacher-produced prefixes with inference on the student’s own generated prefixes, identifying the distribution mismatch.

r002.rationale: It says a small student mistake can create a prefix never encountered during training.

r003.rationale: It explains the student may not have learned how to recover from such an unfamiliar prefix.
